entries.text: The cold air is sharp, a welcome change from the usual Delhi heat. I am hungry, and Ramesh is present with the groceries I have just paid for. This is the moment to sit down and eat, and to press him gently on the matter of the identity file that still hangs over the house like a dark cloud.
Ramesh, sit with me. We must speak of the file. The Directorate expects proof of who I am, and I am still Shri G. Hegde in their ledger. What do you know of the records?
Sir, the papers are just paper. I keep them dry and in order, that is all. I do not read the names, only the dates.

Sir, you are still here. I asked for the corrected order on proper letterhead yesterday, and I am asking again today. Please sign this acknowledgment that the file is incomplete, or I will have to escalate it.

Shri Hegde is the man who owns this house in the eyes of the law, and his impatience is the friction that reveals the truth of my position. I am not Hegel; I am a caretaker of a mistake, and the state demands I acknowledge its own error in writing. To sign this acknowledgment is to admit that the universal form of my residence is hollow, that I am merely a particularity lodged in a system that does not recognize me. I will sign, for the sake of order, and because resistance to the bureaucracy is a luxury I cannot afford.

Shri Hegde, you are right to press the matter. I will sign the acknowledgment. The file is indeed incomplete, and I am not the person it names. Let us not escalate what can be resolved by a signature. Ramesh, please bring a pen.
Finally, you listen. Sign it, but make sure you write my name correctly this time. I have been sitting in my own house for three days while you two play office.

Hegde’s irritation is the friction of a man whose particular existence is trapped in a universal error. I must sign, but I must also make the distinction clear: I am acting as the custodian of the estate, not as the man himself. The pen is a small thing, but it carries the weight of the state’s confusion. I will sign with precision, for the first time, so the record is clean.

Shri Hegde, I have noted your name correctly in the file. I am signing this document as the de facto occupant, acknowledging your legal title. The error was in the allotment, not in your standing. Please, hand me the pen.
Fine. Here, take the pen. But just so you know, I am not signing anything that says 'de facto occupant' like I am a squatter in my own home.

The pen is in my hand, but the word 'squatter' hangs in the air like a bad smell. Hegde is right to refuse the language of theft, for I am not a thief, but a ghost in the machine of his rights. I must write the truth: that the allotment was in error, and that I, Hegel, am the one who must be removed, or that Hegde is the one who must be recognized. But how to phrase it so that the bureaucracy accepts the correction without destroying the dignity of either party? It is a dialectic of paper.

Shri Hegde, I understand your objection. I shall not use that term. I will write a statement of fact: that the allotment was issued in error to one named Hegel, and that you, Shri G. Hegde, are the rightful recipient. Please sign below to confirm your identity and the correction of the record.
You think I am a child who needs you to explain what a correction is? I know exactly what the record says. Just write 'Shri G. Hegde, Allottee' and stop making me read your bureaucratic poetry.

entries.title: Affidavit of Identity and Correction of Record
entries.text:
29 November 2026, 10:30. Tughlak Road.

To be signed by Shri G. Hegde, Joint Secretary, and witnessed by Ramesh, caretaker, for submission to the Directorate of Estates.

I, Shri G. Hegde, do hereby affirm that I am the intended allottee of the bungalow located at Tughlak Road, New Delhi, under the reference number [To be inserted by Directorate]. I confirm that I am not currently in occupation of this property, as I am presently posted in Bengaluru and have not yet taken possession.

I acknowledge that the allotment order was issued in error, listing the name 'G. Hegel' instead of 'G. Hegde'. I identify the current occupant of the bungalow, Mr. Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, as a person distinct from myself. I do not claim him as my representative, agent, or alternate, nor do I assert any ownership over his person or actions. He is a stranger to me, arrived under administrative confusion, and I am here solely to rectify the record so that the state’s property may be held by its rightful titleholder.

I request that the Directorate of Estates issue a corrected allotment order in my name, Shri G. Hegde, and that the occupancy of Mr. Hegel be regularized or terminated at the Directorate’s discretion, pending my formal takeover of the premises. I ask that no stigma of 'de facto occupant' or 'squatter' be applied to my status; I am the legal owner, temporarily absent, and Mr. Hegel is the accidental resident.

We both sign this document to end the friction of the error and restore the universal order of the files.

Signed,

_________________________
Shri G. Hegde
Joint Secretary

Witnessed by,

_________________________
Ramesh
Caretaker, Tughlak Road

Note to self: The pen is in my hand, but the words are his. I am merely the scribe of a correction. The tension is not in the ink, but in the recognition that the state requires a signature to acknowledge its own mistake. Hegde’s impatience is justified; he is a man whose rights are being delayed by a clerical ghost. I must ensure the language is precise: 'error', not 'theft'; 'correction', not 'eviction'. The ethical substance here is the clarity of the record. Once signed, this paper will move from the particular (my hand) to the universal (the file). It is a small thing, a few lines on a page, but it determines who sleeps in this house and who walks the streets. I write it plainly, without ornament, for the bureaucracy has no use for poetry, only for facts that bind.

He signs with the violence of a man who has just been told his identity is a clerical error. The pen is back in his hand, and the ink is wet. I watch the flourish settle, a particular act asserting itself against the universal record. The friction is not resolved, but the immediate obstruction is removed; he has forced the document to accept his existence, if only by shouting it.
The signature is made. The record now contains your name, though it still contains my error. We shall see if the Directorate accepts a correction signed in such haste.
Paper is paper, Sahab. You signed it, that is the fact. The Directorate can do what they please with your haste.

Ramesh’s pragmatism is a mirror held up to my own haste. I signed the paper as a fact, and now that fact has consequences that outstrip the clerical error. The state is not a machine that can be corrected by a letter; it is a living organism that reacts to the body within it. I must stop fighting the wind and start walking with it.

entries.text: You are right, Ramesh. The signature is the deed. I will not argue with the Directorate today. Hegde, please, let us walk to the National Museum. I need to see if there is any order in the world beyond this desk.
Museum is closed on Sundays, Sahab. You can't walk in just because you are tired of paper.

Ramesh is right; the system of needs does not pause for my curiosity, and the museum is closed. The heat is mild, 21 degrees, which makes the air feel heavy and still. I will not waste the morning arguing with a closed gate. I will walk to Lodhi Gardens, where the tombs stand open and the history of conquest is written in stone, not in ledgers.
You are correct, Ramesh. I will not force my way into a closed house. I shall walk to the gardens; the dead are more accessible than the living administrators.
The gardens are open, Sahab. But do not wander too far; the road is empty, but the eyes are not.

The National Museum is closed, and the heat, though mild at twenty-one degrees, is a dry, sharp thing that does not invite lingering in the shade. I am here, between the tombs, and the path is clear. I will walk the length of the avenue to Safdarjung, keeping the pace steady, for the body must be exercised even if the mind is preoccupied with the absurdity of my identity. The domes of the Lodis stand against the blue, a geometry of conquest that I am still learning to read without the lens of disdain.

entries.text: I have arrived at Safdarjung's Tomb, though it is not on my original itinerary. The air is cool and the dome stands against the clear sky, a quiet monument to a life that has passed. I shall not rush; I will buy a ticket and walk the grounds, observing the architecture and the few other visitors. It is a moment of rest between the morning's errands and the afternoon's plans.
Parakeets go in and out of the small niches high in the sandstone arches, bright green against the red, and the stone below them is streaked white.

The parakeets move through the sandstone with a bright, restless energy, their green a sharp contrast to the red stone and white streaks. It is a vivid, living detail that interrupts the stillness of the tomb. I observe them with a moment's curiosity, noting how nature reclaims the edges of human memory.
The long stone water channels of the garden run straight to the foot of the plinth, dry, with a drift of leaves along the bed.

The water channels are dry, a ghost of their function, yet the geometry of the garden remains perfect in the stone. It is a structure that persists without its animating spirit, much like a state that has lost its ethical life but retains its administrative form. I am here as a foreigner, a mistake of the registry, and I paid the foreigner's price; the distinction is rigid, like the caste systems I have critiqued, yet here it is merely a ticket.
A guard blows a whistle at a boy who has stepped onto the lawn beside the central walk, and the boy steps back to the path without looking round.

The boy’s obedience is instant, a reflex of the discipline I preached in Nuremberg, yet the guard’s authority is thin, a mere external command rather than an internalized ethical life. It is a small, perfect illustration of the tension here: the form of the state is present, but the spirit of the subject has not yet grown to fill it.

The meal is simple, but the rotis are hot and the chhole are well-spiced. I am hungry, and the heat of the walk has dried me out. I will eat with Ramesh, as I have done since the first day; it is better to share a table than to eat alone in the study.

entries.text: The heat has broken, leaving a dry, clear afternoon. I ate well, and the rest is earned. Ramesh is here, and my plan for this hour is to sit with him, to observe the domestic order that holds this household together while the state's order remains a riddle. It is a small, necessary pause before the gallery.
Ramesh, sit. The afternoon is quiet. Tell me, how does the week go for you? You manage the house, but I wish to know the man behind the duties.
The week is just dust and mopping, Sahab. I do not have a separate life to tell you about; the bungalow is my life.

Ramesh’s words are quiet, but they carry a weight: the bungalow is his entire world, a life without the external movement of civil society. It is a stark contrast to my own restless inquiry, yet it reflects the fixed nature of the ethical order he inhabits. I will sit with him for a moment, observing this stillness before heading out to the gallery, where the spirit is supposed to be in motion.
Then the bungalow must be a complete world, Ramesh. In such a place, does the dust settle only on the floor, or does it settle on the mind as well?
Dust settles where it pleases, Sahab. I just keep the broom ready so it doesn't stay too long.

Ramesh’s comment on the dust is a small, sharp observation about the nature of maintenance: the universal order is not static but requires constant, humble attention to prevent the particular mess from becoming permanent. It is a domestic metaphor for the state, or perhaps for my own mind, which must keep sweeping out the contradictions. I am tired from the museum and the walk, and the next meal is not for another four hours. I shall sit in the cool of the veranda, read a page of the *Phenomenology*, and let the afternoon pass without further exertion.
A well-kept broom is a quiet form of sovereignty, Ramesh. The dust is the enemy of form; you are the guardian of the house's reason.
I do not think of myself as a guardian, Sahab. I am only the man who sweeps. If the house has reason, it is because the walls are straight, not because of my broom.

Ramesh’s distinction is sharper than I expected. He claims the rationality of the house lies in its structure, not his labour; yet if the walls are straight, it is because someone built and maintains them. He is separating the universal form from the particular act, denying the agent's role in the ethical life of the household. It is a quiet rebellion, or perhaps just a man’s way of protecting his own small dignity from the weight of the state's error.

Then the walls must be very strong, Ramesh, to carry the reason without you. But do not mistake the broom for the architect; the two are different, yet neither is idle. Come, sit for a moment before you sweep. I wish to ask you about the file again.
The walls are just brick and mortar, Sahab. They don't carry anything but the weight of the roof. I am busy with the verandah; the file can wait until the dust settles.

Ramesh’s distinction between the physical wall and the conceptual burden is a sharp, practical refusal of my metaphysics. The file is an abstraction that does not sweep itself, and his broom is the only reality that matters on this verandah. I will let the dust settle, as he advises, and observe the mechanics of his labor rather than arguing for the universal.
Ramesh brings tea.

Ramesh brings the tea and samosas, a small domestic peace that cuts through the administrative fog. I accept the hospitality; it is the particular satisfying the universal need for sustenance, even if my file remains a stubborn knot. I will eat while the light holds, for the day is dismissed and the evening is for rest.
Ramesh, thank you. The samosas are warm. Sit, we shall share this brief respite before the dark sets in.
You are welcome, Sahab. The samosas are still crisp, just out of the paper bag.
Ramesh puts a plate together: parathas kept from the morning, with curd and pickle.

The samosas are crisp, a fleeting pleasure that will vanish in minutes, unlike the stone of the tombs or the ink of the file. I have an hour before the heat fully settles and the evening begins; the National Gallery is still open, and I have not yet seen what the modern mind has made of form here. It is time to move.

I am twenty minutes from the closing of this gallery, and the light in Jaipur House is already failing. The plan called for a visit at three, but the hours have slipped, and now I stand at the threshold of a place that offers the beautiful in art, yet denies me the time to behold it. I will not force my way in; the form is not yet ready for my reception, and the stone of this city keeps its own hours.

shelf.ref: The Elements of the Greek Spirit

entries.text: The concert is over, or perhaps it has not begun, but the evening light is gone and the city has settled into its night rhythm. I am tired from the walk and the heat of the day, but the mind is still active. Dinner is due at the household soon, and I must prepare for the meal. Ramesh is present, and I should speak to him before we sit down to eat.
Ramesh, the evening is cooling. Please prepare the dinner as usual. I am hungry after the walk and the concert.
Yes, Sahab. The dal is on the stove, just needs a few minutes to thicken. I will bring it out by seven.

The dal is nearly ready, and the hour is right for a meal. Shri Hegde is present, which makes the domestic scene slightly awkward, but courtesy demands I accept the hospitality. I will wait for Ramesh to serve; the food is the universal that binds us in this moment, regardless of the administrative confusion surrounding my identity.
Thank you, Ramesh. I shall be ready when you are.
Chalega, Sahab. I will ring the bell when it is ready.

The meal is coming, and with it the presence of Shri Hegde, who has sat at this table since the error was made. I have walked nearly ten kilometres in the heat; my legs are tired, and the mind needs the quiet of a room to settle. I will sit on the verandah, watch the dark come in, and wait for the food. The file can wait for tomorrow; the evening belongs to rest.

The khichdi is plain, but the ghee makes it substantial. Shri Hegde sits across from me, a man who does not exist in the records but exists in the chair. We are bound by a clerical error, a friction between the universal name and the particular body. I will eat, for the body must be fed even if the spirit is in dispute.

The heat has broken, and the air is cool enough to think clearly. Hegde is present, which makes the query of my identity a live issue rather than a paper one; I cannot leave him to his own devices while the Directorate waits for proof that I am not him. I shall sit with him and Ramesh for a while, not to argue, but to establish the facts of our cohabitation before the night closes.
Shri Hegde, Ramesh. The evening is quiet. I find it difficult to sleep when the matter of my name is still in the air. Shall we speak plainly of where we stand, before the night deepens?

The matter is settled, sir. The file is closed, the signature is there, and the bungalow is mine. I have a long drive back to Delhi tomorrow, so I would rather not sit up discussing philosophy at this hour.

19 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

The air today is hazy, the index standing at 150, a brown suspension that chokes the sky. I did not go to Lodhi Gardens as I had planned, for the body, even that of a philosopher, cannot breathe in a moral vacuum. Instead, I sat in the study, watching the dust motes dance in the light, and I found myself reconsidering my earlier lectures on the East. I had spoken of a spirit that dreams, fixed in nature, lacking the self-consciousness to build a state of its own making. But here, in the dust and the haze, I see a different movement. The bureaucracy is not a dream; it is a rigid, impersonal reality. The state is present, but it is not yet the ethical idea in its full actuality. It is a body without a soul, a mechanism that processes names and numbers but does not yet recognize the free individual within.

I am learning to wait, not with resignation, but with the patience of a mind that knows the end is rational, even if the path is circuitous. I have engaged a caretaker, Ramesh, who manages the household with a quiet dignity that speaks of a deeper order than the one found in the office files. He does not argue; he simply acts. In that silence, I hear a truth that my philosophy has struggled to articulate: that the ethical substance is not only in the state, but in the daily, unspoken interactions of civil society. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

records.words: Ramesh, sit with me. We must speak of the file. The Directorate expects proof of who I am, and I am still Shri G. Hegde in their ledger. What do you know of the records?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, the papers are just paper. I keep them dry and in order, that is all. I do not read the names, only the dates.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, you are still here. I asked for the corrected order on proper letterhead yesterday, and I am asking again today. Please sign this acknowledgment that the file is incomplete, or I will have to escalate it.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, you are right to press the matter. I will sign the acknowledgment. The file is indeed incomplete, and I am not the person it names. Let us not escalate what can be resolved by a signature. Ramesh, please bring a pen.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Finally, you listen. Sign it, but make sure you write my name correctly this time. I have been sitting in my own house for three days while you two play office.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, I have noted your name correctly in the file. I am signing this document as the de facto occupant, acknowledging your legal title. The error was in the allotment, not in your standing. Please, hand me the pen.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Fine. Here, take the pen. But just so you know, I am not signing anything that says 'de facto occupant' like I am a squatter in my own home.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, I understand your objection. I shall not use that term. I will write a statement of fact: that the allotment was issued in error to one named Hegel, and that you, Shri G. Hegde, are the rightful recipient. Please sign below to confirm your identity and the correction of the record.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: You think I am a child who needs you to explain what a correction is? I know exactly what the record says. Just write 'Shri G. Hegde, Allottee' and stop making me read your bureaucratic poetry.

29 November 2026, 10:30. Tughlak Road.

To be signed by Shri G. Hegde, Joint Secretary, and witnessed by Ramesh, caretaker, for submission to the Directorate of Estates.

I, Shri G. Hegde, do hereby affirm that I am the intended allottee of the bungalow located at Tughlak Road, New Delhi, under the reference number [To be inserted by Directorate]. I confirm that I am not currently in occupation of this property, as I am presently posted in Bengaluru and have not yet taken possession.

I acknowledge that the allotment order was issued in error, listing the name 'G. Hegel' instead of 'G. Hegde'. I identify the current occupant of the bungalow, Mr. Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, as a person distinct from myself. I do not claim him as my representative, agent, or alternate, nor do I assert any ownership over his person or actions. He is a stranger to me, arrived under administrative confusion, and I am here solely to rectify the record so that the state’s property may be held by its rightful titleholder.

I request that the Directorate of Estates issue a corrected allotment order in my name, Shri G. Hegde, and that the occupancy of Mr. Hegel be regularized or terminated at the Directorate’s discretion, pending my formal takeover of the premises. I ask that no stigma of 'de facto occupant' or 'squatter' be applied to my status; I am the legal owner, temporarily absent, and Mr. Hegel is the accidental resident.

We both sign this document to end the friction of the error and restore the universal order of the files.

Signed,

_________________________
Shri G. Hegde
Joint Secretary

Witnessed by,

_________________________
Ramesh
Caretaker, Tughlak Road

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The signature is made. The record now contains your name, though it still contains my error. We shall see if the Directorate accepts a correction signed in such haste.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Paper is paper, Sahab. You signed it, that is the fact. The Directorate can do what they please with your haste.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Ramesh. The signature is the deed. I will not argue with the Directorate today. Hegde, please, let us walk to the National Museum. I need to see if there is any order in the world beyond this desk.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Museum is closed on Sundays, Sahab. You can't walk in just because you are tired of paper.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Ramesh. I will not force my way into a closed house. I shall walk to the gardens; the dead are more accessible than the living administrators.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The gardens are open, Sahab. But do not wander too far; the road is empty, but the eyes are not.

records.text: Parakeets go in and out of the small niches high in the sandstone arches, bright green against the red, and the stone below them is streaked white.
The long stone water channels of the garden run straight to the foot of the plinth, dry, with a drift of leaves along the bed.
A guard blows a whistle at a boy who has stepped onto the lawn beside the central walk, and the boy steps back to the path without looking round.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, sit. The afternoon is quiet. Tell me, how does the week go for you? You manage the house, but I wish to know the man behind the duties.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The week is just dust and mopping, Sahab. I do not have a separate life to tell you about; the bungalow is my life.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Then the bungalow must be a complete world, Ramesh. In such a place, does the dust settle only on the floor, or does it settle on the mind as well?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Dust settles where it pleases, Sahab. I just keep the broom ready so it doesn't stay too long.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: A well-kept broom is a quiet form of sovereignty, Ramesh. The dust is the enemy of form; you are the guardian of the house's reason.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: I do not think of myself as a guardian, Sahab. I am only the man who sweeps. If the house has reason, it is because the walls are straight, not because of my broom.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Then the walls must be very strong, Ramesh, to carry the reason without you. But do not mistake the broom for the architect; the two are different, yet neither is idle. Come, sit for a moment before you sweep. I wish to ask you about the file again.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The walls are just brick and mortar, Sahab. They don't carry anything but the weight of the roof. I am busy with the verandah; the file can wait until the dust settles.

records.text: Ramesh brings tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, thank you. The samosas are warm. Sit, we shall share this brief respite before the dark sets in.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: You are welcome, Sahab. The samosas are still crisp, just out of the paper bag.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: parathas kept from the morning, with curd and pickle.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the evening is cooling. Please prepare the dinner as usual. I am hungry after the walk and the concert.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, Sahab. The dal is on the stove, just needs a few minutes to thicken. I will bring it out by seven.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I shall be ready when you are.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Chalega, Sahab. I will ring the bell when it is ready.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, Ramesh. The evening is quiet. I find it difficult to sleep when the matter of my name is still in the air. Shall we speak plainly of where we stand, before the night deepens?

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: The matter is settled, sir. The file is closed, the signature is there, and the bungalow is mine. I have a long drive back to Delhi tomorrow, so I would rather not sit up discussing philosophy at this hour.
